name: MinIO
license: AGPLv3 (community edition, now archived); AIStor is proprietary

archived.reason: MinIO, Inc. stopped publishing community binaries in October 2025 and archived the open-source `minio/minio` repository on 25 April 2026. In September 2026 the `minio/minio` and `minio/mc` images disappeared from Docker Hub, so `docker pull minio/minio` now fails. Existing servers keep running but get no fixes. For anything new, pick a maintained alternative below.

summary: A self-hosted object store that speaks the S3 API. The open-source edition is archived and its images are gone from Docker Hub; MinIO now sells AIStor.
intro: MinIO is an object storage server you run on your own machines or Kubernetes cluster. Applications talk to it with the S3 API, so the AWS SDKs, the `aws` CLI, Spark, Trino and backup tools work by changing only the endpoint URL. A deployment spreads each object across many drives and servers with erasure coding, so it survives lost disks or nodes without keeping full copies. Admins use the `mc` command-line client for buckets, users, policies, lifecycle rules and event notifications.

The open-source edition has been licensed under the AGPLv3 since 2021, and the company has steadily pulled back from it. In 2025 the community build lost its web admin console, keeping only a basic object browser. In October 2025 it switched to source-only releases with no pre-built binaries, and in December it went into maintenance mode. On 25 April 2026 the `minio/minio` GitHub repository was archived and marked “no longer maintained”, and in September 2026 the `minio/minio` and `minio/mc` images vanished from Docker Hub. The README now points users to AIStor, MinIO’s commercial S3-compatible product, which comes as AIStor Free or AIStor Enterprise.
strengths: S3-compatible, so the same code runs against AWS and your own hardware
Runs anywhere: bare metal, VMs, Kubernetes, air-gapped sites
Erasure coding tolerates failed drives and nodes without full replicas
Bucket notifications can publish to Kafka, AMQP, Redis, PostgreSQL, webhooks and more
limits: Archived: no maintained builds or security fixes, and `docker pull minio/minio` and `minio/mc` fail because the images are gone from Docker Hub
Building from the archived source still works, but you own every patch from then on; the `mc` client repository is archived too
You run the hardware, capacity planning, upgrades and durability yourself

snippet.title: Manage a MinIO deployment with mc, then use any S3 client
source: mc event add lab/backups arn:minio:sqs::primary:kafka --event put
# any S3 client works by pointing it at MinIO

sections.title: Where to go from MinIO
sections.intro: Every option below is maintained. Pick by what you used MinIO for; each has its own page with a “Moving from MinIO” section where it applies.

items.name: PGSTY Silo
items.text: The open-source MinIO server, still maintained by the Pigsty community. Same S3 API, `MINIO_*` settings and data on disk; the binary is `silo` and the image is `pgsty/silo` on Docker Hub. Switch every node at once. AGPLv3.

items.name: RustFS
items.text: A Rust reimplementation of MinIO’s design, with the same ports and storage model and tools to import MinIO’s bucket metadata and IAM. Apache 2.0, but 1.0 only shipped in September 2026, and running on MinIO’s existing drives is still a preview.

items.name: SeaweedFS
items.text: Mature and fast with billions of small files, and serves the same data over S3 and a FUSE file system. More components to run than MinIO, and no S3 bucket notifications or replication API. Apache 2.0.

items.name: Ceph (RADOS Gateway)
items.text: The heavyweight: S3 buckets, block devices and a file system from one pool of disks, with versioning, Object Lock and multisite replication. Needs at least three hosts and real operations skill. Runs on Kubernetes through Rook.

items.name: Garage
items.text: A light server for a few nodes spread across sites on ordinary internet links. Covers plain bucket storage only: no versioning, Object Lock, bucket policies or notifications. AGPLv3.

items.name: Versity S3 Gateway
items.text: Puts an S3 API in front of an existing file system or object store and keeps objects as plain files. The replacement for MinIO’s gateway mode, which MinIO removed in 2022, rather than for a MinIO cluster. Apache 2.0.

items.name: Apache Ozone
items.text: Serves the same buckets over S3 and as a Hadoop file system, for teams whose MinIO fed Spark, Hive or Trino. Heavier to run, and its S3 gateway lacks versioning, Object Lock and bucket policies. Apache 2.0.

items.name: Zenko CloudServer
items.text: Scality’s Node.js S3 server, a light single-container stand-in for MinIO in tests and Compose files. Not for production clusters: one node, no replication. Current images are at `ghcr.io/scality/cloudserver`.

items.name: AIStor
items.text: MinIO’s commercial product and the path its README recommends: AIStor Free is a standalone edition under a free licence, and AIStor Enterprise is the distributed edition with commercial support. Proprietary licence.

items.name: A managed service
items.text: If you only self-hosted to get an S3 endpoint, Amazon S3, Cloudflare R2, Google Cloud Storage or Azure Blob Storage remove the servers entirely. R2 has no egress fees.

items.name: Build the archived code
items.text: `go install github.com/minio/minio@latest` or the repository’s Dockerfile still produce a working server, but nobody publishes fixes any more, so you take on every security patch yourself.

story: MinIO’s idea was a small server that speaks Amazon’s S3 API on your own hardware, so software written for S3 could run anywhere. AB Periasamy, who had earlier co-founded Gluster (a distributed file system Red Hat agreed to buy for about $136 million in 2011), started MinIO in 2014 with Garima Kapoor and Harshavardhana. The first commit to `minio/minio` landed on 31 October 2014, and the first official release in June 2015 was billed as “Minimalist Object Storage”.

Written in Go and released under the Apache License 2.0, it became one of the most popular self-hosted object stores, with more than 60,000 GitHub stars. In April 2021 MinIO relicensed it under the AGPLv3, which obliges anyone who modifies it and offers it over a network to publish their changes, and pointed commercial users at a paid licence.

From 2025 the company pulled back from the open-source edition. A change opened in February 2025 cut the community console down to an object browser; in October the project went source-only, with no more binaries; in December it entered maintenance mode; and on 25 April 2026 the repository was archived with a README pointing users to AIStor. In September 2026 the `minio/minio` and `minio/mc` images disappeared from Docker Hub, breaking the many Compose files and CI jobs that pulled them. Community forks such as Silo now carry the open-source server forward.

choices.choice: Speak the S3 API, not a new one
choices.why: Code written for AWS, from SDKs and the `aws` CLI to Spark and backup tools, runs against MinIO by changing only the endpoint, so moving data on-premises needs no rewrite.

choices.choice: Erasure coding instead of full copies
choices.why: Splitting each object into data and parity pieces across drives and servers survives lost disks or nodes while using less raw capacity than keeping several full replicas.

Under Apache 2.0 anyone could repackage MinIO without contributing back. The AGPL requires releasing modified code to network users, which pushed companies that wanted proprietary use towards a commercial licence.
